entry: British statesman and Conservative politician; Prime Minister of the United Kingdom (1868; 1874–1880). Disraeli played a central role in creating the modern [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] and defined its policies. He made the Conservatives the party most identified with the [[British Empire]] and with military action to expand it. He was the only British prime minister born into a Jewish family; his father left Judaism after a dispute at his [[Synagogue|synagogue]], and Disraeli became an Anglican at age 11. After entering the House of Commons in 1837, he rose to prominence by clashing with [[Robert Peel]] over repeal of the Corn Laws. In his second term he arranged for Britain to buy a major interest in the [[Suez Canal]] Company, and at the [[Congress of Berlin]] in 1878 he secured peace in the Balkans on terms favorable to Britain and unfavorable to Russia. He maintained a close friendship with [[Queen Victoria]], who made him Earl of Beaconsfield in 1876.

American [[Polymath|polymath]] and Founding Father. Franklin was a successful printer and newspaper editor in [[Philadelphia]], publishing *Poor Richard's Almanack* and the *Pennsylvania Gazette*. He was a drafter and signer of the Declaration of Independence and the first postmaster general. As an agent in London for several colonies, he spearheaded repeal of the Stamp Act. As the first U.S. ambassador to France, he secured vital French support for the [[American Revolutionary War]], and he signed the [[Treaty of Paris (1783)|Treaty of Paris]] with Britain. His studies of electricity made him a major figure in the history of physics; his inventions included the [[Lightning|lightning]] rod, bifocals and the glass harmonica. He also charted and named the [[Gulf Stream]]. Franklin owned at least seven slaves from at least 1735, but by the late 1750s he argued against slavery and became an active abolitionist. He was the first president of the Academy and College of Philadelphia, which later became the [[University of Pennsylvania]].

Republican politician and 23rd president of the United States (1889–1893). A Union army veteran and grandson of the ninth president, William Henry Harrison, he defeated incumbent [[Grover Cleveland]] in 1888 by winning the Electoral College while losing the popular vote. His administration enacted the McKinley Tariff and the Sherman Antitrust Act, and six western states were admitted to the Union. Federal spending reached $1 billion for the first time, an issue that helped cost Republicans the 1890 midterm elections. Cleveland defeated him in 1892.

French dancer and choreographer. Born in [[Bordeaux]], he joined the New York City Ballet in 1995, became a principal dancer in 2002 and retired from the company in 2011. He choreographed and performed as a dancer in the film *Black Swan* (2010) and made his feature directorial debut with *Carmen*. He founded the L.A. Dance Project in 2011 and was director of dance at the Paris Opera Ballet from 2014 to 2016. He was married to [[Natalie Portman]] until their divorce was finalized in 2024.

Israeli politician and diplomat; prime minister of Israel (1996–1999; 2009–2021; since 2022). Israel's longest-serving prime minister, he was born in [[Tel Aviv]] and served in the Israel Defense Forces. He became chair of [[Likud]] in 1993, and in 1996 he was elected the first Israeli prime minister chosen by direct popular vote. He made his closeness to [[Donald Trump]] central to his appeal; during Trump's first presidency the United States recognized Jerusalem as Israel's capital and brokered the Abraham Accords. Expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied [[West Bank]], deemed illegal under international law, drew criticism, and critics argue that his governments have shown democratic backsliding. In 2019 he was indicted on charges of breach of trust, bribery and fraud, which he denies. In November 2024 the [[International Criminal Court]] issued an arrest warrant for him over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Polish-born French-American mathematician and a leading figure in fractal geometry. He coined the term *fractal* and developed a theory of "roughness and self-similarity" in nature. Working at [[IBM]] for 35 years from 1958, he used computer graphics to display fractal images and discovered the [[Mandelbrot set]] in 1979–1980. He taught at [[Harvard University]] and was Sterling Professor of Mathematical Sciences at [[Yale University]], where he was the oldest professor in the university's history to receive tenure. His research spanned fields from [[Economics|economics]] to [[Meteorology|meteorology]], [[Linguistics|linguistics]] and medicine. He received more than 15 honorary doctorates. His autobiography, *The Fractalist*, was published posthumously in 2012.

Colorless, flammable aromatic [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbon]] with the formula C₆H₆. Its molecule is a planar hexagonal ring of six carbon atoms, each bonded to one hydrogen atom. Benzene is a natural constituent of petroleum and one of the elementary [[Petrochemical|petrochemicals]]. It is produced industrially by catalytic reforming and steam cracking, and used mainly as a precursor for chemicals such as ethylbenzene and cumene, and for styrene, which makes [[Polystyrene|polystyrene]] plastics. [[Michael Faraday]] first isolated it in 1825, and in 1865 Friedrich August Kekulé proposed its ring structure. Benzene is classified as a [[Carcinogen|carcinogen]]; chronic exposure is linked to bone marrow suppression and [[Leukemia|leukemia]].

Class of central nervous system depressant drugs, colloquially called "benzos". Benzodiazepines enhance the effect of the [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitter]] gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) at the GABAA receptor, producing sedative, hypnotic, anxiolytic and anticonvulsant effects. They are prescribed for [[Anxiety disorder|anxiety disorders]], [[Insomnia|insomnia]] and seizures. The first, chlordiazepoxide (Librium), was discovered accidentally by Leo Sternbach in 1955 and marketed in 1960; diazepam (Valium) followed in 1963. Long-term use is controversial because of dependence, withdrawal and concerns about [[Dementia|dementia]] and [[Cancer|cancer]]. Combined with [[Alcohol (drug)|alcohol]] or [[Opioid|opioids]], they greatly increase the risk of fatal overdose. They are controlled in most countries.

[[Old English]] epic poem of 3,182 alliterative lines in the tradition of Germanic heroic legend. Set in pagan [[Scandinavia|Scandinavia]], it tells how the Geatish hero Beowulf kills the monster Grendel, who has terrorized the mead hall Heorot, and then defeats Grendel's mother. Beowulf later becomes king of the Geats and, fifty years on, is mortally wounded in killing a dragon. Scholars debate whether the poem was composed orally in pagan times or later by a Christian author, which determines whether its pagan elements are central or decorative. The only surviving copy, the Nowell Codex, was damaged by fire in 1731 and is held by the British Library. The poem was first transcribed in 1786, and hundreds of translations have been made since 1900, including by [[J. R. R. Tolkien]], who wrote an essay on translating it.

Branch of the [[Afroasiatic languages|Afroasiatic]] language family spoken in North Africa, also called Amazigh or Tamazight. The languages form a dialect continuum with a level of variety similar to the [[Romance languages]]. Millions of people in [[Morocco]] and [[Algeria]] speak them natively, with smaller populations in [[Libya]], [[Tunisia]], [[Mali]], Niger, Mauritania and Burkina Faso. Historically written in the ancient Libyco-Berber script, they are now written in Tifinagh, the Berber Latin alphabet or the [[Arabic script]], with Latin the most widespread. Suppressed and of low prestige since the 1950s, the languages gained recognition when Morocco and Algeria made Tamazight an official language in their constitutions in 2011 and 2016 respectively.

Ethnic group indigenous to [[North Africa]]. Also called Amazigh or Imazighen, Berbers are linked mainly by their use of [[Berber languages]], part of the Afroasiatic family. Most live in the [[Maghreb]], in Morocco, Algeria, Libya and Tunisia, with smaller communities in Mali, Niger, Mauritania and Egypt's Siwa Oasis. Many view the exonym "Berber", related to the Arabic word for "barbarian", as pejorative. Berber kingdoms such as Numidia and Mauretania were eventually suppressed by the Arab conquests of the 7th and 8th centuries AD, which began a long process of Arabization and conversion to [[Islam]]. Berber dynasties, including the Almoravids and Almohads, nevertheless ruled much of North Africa and the [[Iberian Peninsula]] from the 11th to 16th centuries.

Fragrant citrus fruit (*Citrus bergamia*) the size of an orange. Genetic research suggests it is a probable hybrid of [[Lemon|lemon]] and bitter orange. Grown mainly in Calabria, Italy, which accounts for over 90% of global production, it yields an aromatic rind oil used in [[Perfume|perfumes]], [[Cosmetics|cosmetics]] and [[Tea|Earl Grey tea]]. Use of the oil on the skin can increase photosensitivity, resulting in greater damage from sun exposure.

Marginal sea of the northern [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]] between Alaska and Russia. Named after the Danish-born Russian navigator [[Vitus Bering]], who first systematically explored it in 1728, the sea is separated from the Gulf of Alaska by the Alaska Peninsula. It connects to the Arctic Ocean through the [[Bering Strait]], and together with the strait it forms the divide between Eurasia and the Americas. The sea has a deep central basin that rises to shallower continental shelves. The interaction of currents, sea ice and weather makes for a vigorous and productive ecosystem, including international waters known as the "Donut Hole".

Strait between Asia and North America, linking the [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific]] and [[Arctic Ocean|Arctic]] oceans. It separates Russia's Chukchi Peninsula from Alaska's Seward Peninsula, and the Russia–United States maritime boundary runs through it, slightly south of the [[Arctic Circle]]. The strait is named after [[Vitus Bering]]. When glaciers lowered sea levels and exposed a land bridge called Beringia, humans may have migrated from Asia to North America across it. This view of how [[Paleo-Indians]] entered the Americas remains the most widely accepted one.

Ceremonial county in South East England (pop., 2024: 992,327). Reading is the county town and largest settlement. The population is concentrated in the east, near [[Greater London|London]], while the west is rural. [[Windsor Castle]], built after the [[Norman Conquest]], became the official country residence of the British monarch. The Berkshire Downs, a chalk downland, occupy the west of the county.

American multinational conglomerate holding company based in [[Omaha, Nebraska|Omaha]]. Originally a textile manufacturer, it became a conglomerate from 1965 under chairman and CEO [[Warren Buffett]]. Its businesses include [[Insurance|insurance]] and [[Rail transport|freight rail]], and it also holds stakes in publicly traded companies. In August 2024 it became the first non-technology company valued at over $1 trillion. Its Class A shares, the highest-priced of any public company, reached $700,000 in August 2024, as the board has long opposed stock splits.

Cold War barrier around West Berlin (1961–1989). Built by the East German government from August 13, 1961, the guarded concrete wall, with guard towers and a cleared "death strip", was meant to prevent East German citizens from fleeing to the West. Some 3.5 million East Germans, about 20% of the population, had defected before its construction. Over 100,000 people attempted to escape, and estimated deaths at the wall range from 136 to more than 200. Willy Brandt, mayor of West Berlin, called it the "Wall of Shame". After revolutions in [[Eastern Bloc|Eastern Bloc]] countries and mass unrest, the East German government opened the border on November 9, 1989. Demolition began in June 1990, and [[German reunification|German reunification]] followed on October 3, 1990.

Capital and largest city of [[Germany]] (pop., 2025: 3,700,577). It was first documented in the 13th century at the crossing of important trade routes. Berlin served as capital of the [[Kingdom of Prussia]] (1701–1918), the [[German Empire]] (1871–1918), the [[Weimar Republic]] (1919–1933) and [[Nazi Germany]] (1933–1945). After World War II it was divided, and East Berlin became capital of East Germany while West Berlin was cut off by the [[Berlin Wall]]. Following [[German reunification]] in 1990 it again became capital of all Germany. Its economy is based on high technology, services and creative industries. The city is home to [[Humboldt University of Berlin]] and three UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

[[British Overseas Territories|British Overseas Territory]] in the North Atlantic. Bermuda is an [[Archipelago|archipelago]] of 181 islands, most joined by bridges to appear as one landmass, with a land area of 54 sq km. Its tropical climate is moderated by warm, moist ocean air, and a [[Coral reef|coral reef]] offers some protection from [[Tropical cyclone|tropical cyclones]]. The nearest land outside the territory is in [[North Carolina]], about 1,035 km to the west-northwest. Bermuda is a self-governing parliamentary democracy with its capital at Hamilton. Its House of Assembly, dating from 1620, is one of the world's oldest legislatures. The [[United Kingdom]] is responsible for foreign affairs and defense. A 1995 independence referendum produced a large majority against independence.

Loosely defined area of the North Atlantic, roughly bounded by [[Bermuda]], [[Florida]] and [[Puerto Rico]]. Since the mid-20th century it has been the focus of an urban legend that many aircraft, ships and people vanished there mysteriously. The U.S. Coast Guard and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration have stated that disappearance rates there are not statistically higher than in other heavily trafficked waters. Causes cited include the [[Gulf Stream|Gulf Stream]], sudden rogue waves, methane gas hydrates and human error.

Federal city and de facto capital of [[Switzerland]] (pop., 2024: about 146,000). Probably founded in 1191 by the Zähringer ruling family, Bern joined the Swiss Confederacy in 1353 and became the federal city in 1848. Its medieval old town, with sandstone buildings and covered arcades, was designated a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1983.

French businessman, chairman and [[Chief executive officer|chief executive officer]] of [[LVMH]], the world's largest luxury goods company. He trained in [[Civil engineering|civil engineering]]. In 1984 he acquired the textile group Boussac Saint-Frères, which owned the Christian Dior fashion house. In 1987 he helped create LVMH by merging Louis Vuitton with Moët Hennessy. As of December 2025, [[Forbes]] estimated his net worth at US$190.4 billion.

British Army field marshal, 1st Viscount Montgomery of Alamein. He was shot through the lung at the First Battle of Ypres in World War I and later fought at Passchendaele. In World War II he commanded the Eighth Army from August 1942, halting [[Erwin Rommel|Rommel]]'s advance at El Alamein, and commanded all Allied ground forces in the [[Normandy]] campaign from June 6 to September 1, 1944. On May 4, 1945, he accepted the German surrender in north-western Europe at Lüneburg Heath. The failed attempt to cross the Rhine in [[Operation Market Garden]] was among his setbacks. Critics argue that he claimed undue credit for victories. He served as deputy Supreme Allied Commander Europe of [[NATO]] until 1958.

German mathematician known for work in analysis, number theory and differential geometry. He gave the first rigorous formulation of the integral, the Riemann integral, and worked on [[Fourier series|Fourier series]]. His introduction of Riemann surfaces gave complex analysis a natural geometric treatment. His 1859 paper on the prime-counting function contained the original statement of the [[Riemann hypothesis|Riemann hypothesis]] and is regarded as a foundation of [[Analytic number theory|analytic number theory]]. His work in differential geometry laid foundations for the mathematics of [[General relativity|general relativity]]. His career was cut short by [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]].

American stand-up comedian and actor, born Bernard Jeffrey McCullough. He starred in the television series *The Bernie Mac Show* (2001–2006), earning two Emmy Award nominations for lead actor in a comedy series. He played Frank Catton in the *Ocean's* film series and starred in *Bad Santa*. He was one of the "Big Four" comedians in *The Original Kings of Comedy*. He died in [[Chicago]] of complications from [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]].
